title: Optimization Dynamics Imprint Semantic Specificity in Contrastive Embedding Norms
claim: Whether an update pushes a parameter outward or inward is set by the angle between two vectors in a tangent space.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, zoom arrow linking sphere view to tangent plane
description: A two-panel geometric sketch. Panel A, titled 'NTK transmission at X', shows an arc of a sphere with origin O at the bottom left. Two black arrows run from O to the arc: one is the unit embedding \hat z_t(X), the other is the transported direction K^T \hat z_t(x). The angle φ is marked between them. A small blue-shaded tangent patch T_X at the top of the arc holds a red arrow a_K. A grey curved arrow labeled 'zoom of T_X' leads to Panel B. Panel B, 'Tangent hyperplane', shows a larger blue-shaded plane with origin O_T. A blue arrow −s̄(X) and a red arrow a_K start at O_T, and the angle ψ is marked between them. Text below the plane reads 'cos ψ: update alignment' and 'sin φ: concept direction alignment'. The colors are blue for the tangent plane and update vector, and red for a_K. The eye lands first on the red and blue arrows.
caption: Sphere geometry of the radial drift term. At a training sample $X$, the transported radial direction $\mathcal K(x,X)^\top\hat z(x)$ has tangent projection $a_K$ in $T_X\mathbb S^{d-1}$. The source update $-\bar{s}(X)$ also lies in this tangent space. Its angle $\psi_K$ with $a_K$ sets the sign of the radial vote: $\cos\psi_K>0$ pushes $x$ outward, while $\cos\psi_K<0$ pushes it inward.
abstract: Contrastive embedding models trained with scale-invariant losses are typically paired with distance metrics like cosine similarity, effectively ignoring embedding magnitudes. However, surprisingly, empirical studies reveal that despite this, these "discarded" norms seem to correlate with semantic properties such as concept specificity, token frequency, and human uncertainty. In this work, we provide a formal theoretical framework explaining this phenomenon. By analyzing the optimization dynamics, we derive an analytic formula demonstrating that embedding length naturally encodes this information as a byproduct of the training process. We also show how this gives rise to signals that can serve as "free" calibration tools in specific models and retrieval tasks, providing a grounded explanation for a previously heuristic observation.
